techniques.name: SHapley Additive exPlanations
techniques.description: SHAP explains model predictions by quantifying how much each input feature contributes to the outcome. It assigns an importance score to every feature, indicating whether it pushes the prediction towards or away from the average. The method systematically evaluates how predictions change as features are included or excluded, drawing on game theory concepts to ensure a fair distribution of contributions.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing a customer churn prediction model to understand why a specific high-value customer was flagged as likely to leave, revealing that recent support ticket interactions and declining purchase frequency were the main drivers.

Auditing a loan approval model by comparing SHAP values for applicants from different demographic groups, ensuring that protected characteristics like race or gender do not have an undue influence on credit decisions.

limitations.description: Assumes feature independence, which can produce misleading explanations when features are highly correlated, as the model may attribute importance to features that are merely proxies for others.
Computationally expensive for models with many features or large datasets, as the number of required predictions grows exponentially with the number of features.
The choice of background dataset for generating explanations can significantly influence the results, requiring careful selection to ensure a representative baseline.
Global explanations derived from averaging local SHAP values may obscure important heterogeneous effects where features impact subgroups of the population differently.

resources.title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions
resources.abstract: Understanding why a model makes a certain prediction can be as crucial as the prediction's accuracy in many applications. However, the highest accuracy for large modern datasets is often achieved by complex models that even experts struggle to interpret, such as ensemble or deep learning models, creating a tension between accuracy and interpretability. In response, various methods have recently been proposed to help users interpret the predictions of complex models, but it is often unclear how these methods are related and when one method is preferable over another. To address this problem, we present a unified framework for interpreting predictions, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). SHAP assigns each feature an importance value for a particular prediction. Its novel components include: (1) the identification of a new class of additive feature importance measures, and (2) theoretical results showing there is a unique solution in this class with a set of desirable properties. The new class unifies six existing methods, notable because several recent methods in the class lack the proposed desirable properties. Based on insights from this unification, we present new methods that show improved computational performance and/or better consistency with human intuition than previous approaches.

resources.title: From local explanations to global understanding with explainable AI for trees
resources.abstract: Tree-based machine learning models such as random forests, decision trees and gradient boosted trees are popular nonlinear predictive models, yet comparatively little attention has been paid to explaining their predictions. Here we improve the interpretability of tree-based models through three main contributions. (1) A polynomial time algorithm to compute optimal explanations based on game theory. (2) A new type of explanation that directly measures local feature interaction effects. (3) A new set of tools for understanding global model structure based on combining many local explanations of each prediction. We apply these tools to three medical machine learning problems and show how combining many high-quality local explanations allows us to represent global structure while retaining local faithfulness to the original model. These tools enable us to (1) identify high-magnitude but low-frequency nonlinear mortality risk factors in the US population, (2) highlight distinct population subgroups with shared risk characteristics, (3) identify nonlinear interaction effects among risk factors for chronic kidney disease and (4) monitor a machine learning model deployed in a hospital by identifying which features are degrading the model’s performance over time. Given the popularity of tree-based machine learning models, these improvements to their interpretability have implications across a broad set of domains. Tree-based machine learning models are widely used in domains such as healthcare, finance and public services. The authors present an explanation method for trees that enables the computation of optimal local explanations for individual predictions, and demonstrate their method on three medical datasets.

resources.title: An introduction to explainable AI with Shapley values — SHAP documentation
Explainable machine-learning predictions for the prevention of hypoxaemia during surgery
resources.abstract: Although anaesthesiologists strive to avoid hypoxaemia during surgery, reliably predicting future intraoperative hypoxaemia is not possible at present. Here, we report the development and testing of a machine-learning-based system that predicts the risk of hypoxaemia and provides explanations of the risk factors in real time during general anaesthesia. The system, which was trained on minute-by-minute data from the electronic medical records of over 50,000 surgeries, improved the performance of anaesthesiologists by providing interpretable hypoxaemia risks and contributing factors. The explanations for the predictions are broadly consistent with the literature and with prior knowledge from anaesthesiologists. Our results suggest that if anaesthesiologists currently anticipate 15% of hypoxaemia events, with the assistance of this system they could anticipate 30%, a large portion of which may benefit from early intervention because they are associated with modifiable factors. The system can help improve the clinical understanding of hypoxaemia risk during anaesthesia care by providing general insights into the exact changes in risk induced by certain characteristics of the patient or procedure. An alert system based on machine learning and trained on surgical data from electronic medical records helps anaesthesiologists prevent hypoxaemia during surgery by providing interpretable real-time predictions.

techniques.name: Integrated Gradients
techniques.description: Integrated Gradients explains a single prediction of a differentiable model, such as a neural network, by giving each input feature a score for how much it moved the output away from a chosen reference input called the baseline. It applies to any input the model treats as continuous: image pixels, table columns, or, for language models, the vector representation (embedding) of each token, since the token identifiers themselves cannot be interpolated. The method builds a series of inputs along a straight line from the baseline (for example a black image, an all-zero embedding or a sequence of padding tokens) to the actual input, computes the model's gradient at each step, and multiplies each feature's average gradient by that feature's difference from the baseline. The scores satisfy completeness: they sum to the difference between the model's output on the input and on the baseline, which also gives a check that enough steps were used. The output is one score per pixel, feature or token, usually shown as a heatmap or highlighted text, and it means something only relative to the baseline chosen.

example_use_cases.description: An eye-screening programme evaluating a diabetic retinopathy grading model shows graders an Integrated Gradients heatmap beside each prediction, so they can see whether the regions driving a referral are lesions such as haemorrhages rather than camera artefacts, and uses the review to decide whether the model may assist grading.

A team building a question-answering assistant over an organisation's policy documents attributes each answer to the question's tokens and flags questions where the content words receive almost no attribution; those questions become test cases in which the content words are changed, to show whether the assistant actually reads the question.

A trust-and-safety team investigating false positives in a toxic-content classifier aggregates token attributions over wrongly flagged posts to see whether identity terms, such as the name of a religion or a sexual orientation, rather than abusive language drive the score, and adds counter-examples to the training data where they do.

A lender's model-risk team runs Integrated Gradients over a classifier that reads the free-text statements in loan applications, ranking the most highly attributed words across a sample of declined applications to check whether words that reveal a protected characteristic, or stand in for one, carry weight in the decision.

limitations.description: Attributions are measured against the baseline and no choice is neutral. Features that match the baseline score near zero even when the model relies on them: with a black-image baseline, dark pixels on the object get little credit. A comparison of blurred, noise and training-data baselines found none best, so the baseline is an assumption to state and to vary before drawing conclusions.

Requires gradient access to a differentiable model, so it cannot explain tree ensembles, rule-based components or a model reached only through an API. For text, the path runs through token embeddings whose intermediate points are not real words, and subword tokenisation splits a word across several scores that must be recombined before a reviewer can read them.

Each explanation needs one gradient computation per step along the path; the original authors found 20 to 300 steps were usually enough for the scores to sum to within 5% of the output difference. Explaining long documents, high-resolution images or a large audit sample therefore costs tens to hundreds of forward and backward passes per prediction.

A score shows how sensitive the output was to a feature along one straight path, not that the feature causes the outcome in the world or that removing it would change the decision. Maps over neighbouring pixels or tokens are often noisy, and a plausible-looking heatmap does not show that the model's reasoning is sound.

resources.title: Axiomatic Attribution for Deep Networks
resources.abstract: We study the problem of attributing the prediction of a deep network to its input features, a problem previously studied by several other works. We identify two fundamental axioms---Sensitivity and Implementation Invariance that attribution methods ought to satisfy. We show that they are not satisfied by most known attribution methods, which we consider to be a fundamental weakness of those methods. We use the axioms to guide the design of a new attribution method called Integrated Gradients. Our method requires no modification to the original network and is extremely simple to implement; it just needs a few calls to the standard gradient operator. We apply this method to a couple of image models, a couple of text models and a chemistry model, demonstrating its ability to debug networks, to extract rules from a network, and to enable users to engage with models better.

resources.title: Using a Deep Learning Algorithm and Integrated Gradients Explanation to Assist Grading for Diabetic Retinopathy
resources.abstract: PURPOSE: To understand the impact of deep learning diabetic retinopathy (DR) algorithms on physician readers in computer-assisted settings. DESIGN: Evaluation of diagnostic technology. PARTICIPANTS: One thousand seven hundred ninety-six retinal fundus images from 1612 diabetic patients. METHODS: Ten ophthalmologists (5 general ophthalmologists, 4 retina specialists, 1 retina fellow) read images for DR severity based on the International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy disease severity scale in each of 3 conditions: unassisted, grades only, or grades plus heatmap. Grades-only assistance comprised a histogram of DR predictions (grades) from a trained deep-learning model. For grades plus heatmap, we additionally showed explanatory heatmaps. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: For each experiment arm, we computed sensitivity and specificity of each reader and the algorithm for different levels of DR severity against an adjudicated reference standard. We also measured accuracy (exact 5-class level agreement and Cohen's quadratically weighted κ), reader-reported confidence (5-point Likert scale), and grading time. RESULTS: Readers graded more accurately with model assistance than without for the grades-only condition (P < 0.001). Grades plus heatmaps improved accuracy for patients with DR (P < 0.001), but reduced accuracy for patients without DR (P = 0.006). Both forms of assistance increased readers' sensitivity moderate-or-worse DR: unassisted: mean, 79.4% [95% confidence interval (CI), 72.3%-86.5%]; grades only: mean, 87.5% [95% CI, 85.1%-89.9%]; grades plus heatmap: mean, 88.7% [95% CI, 84.9%-92.5%] without a corresponding drop in specificity (unassisted: mean, 96.6% [95% CI, 95.9%-97.4%]; grades only: mean, 96.1% [95% CI, 95.5%-96.7%]; grades plus heatmap: mean, 95.5% [95% CI, 94.8%-96.1%]). Algorithmic assistance increased the accuracy of retina specialists above that of the unassisted reader or model alone; and increased grading confidence and grading time across all readers. For most cases, grades plus heatmap was only as effective as grades only. Over the course of the experiment, grading time decreased across all conditions, although most sharply for grades plus heatmap. CONCLUSIONS: Deep learning algorithms can improve the accuracy of, and confidence in, DR diagnosis in an assisted read setting. They also may increase grading time, although these effects may be ameliorated with experience.

techniques.name: DeepLIFT
techniques.description: DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures) explains neural network predictions by decomposing the difference between the actual output and a reference output back to individual input features. It compares each neuron's activation to a reference activation (typically from a baseline input like all zeros or the dataset mean) and propagates these differences backwards through the network using chain rule modifications. Unlike gradient-based methods, DeepLIFT satisfies the sensitivity property (zero input gets zero attribution) and provides more stable attributions by using discrete differences rather than gradients.

example_use_cases.description: Identifying which genomic sequences contribute to a neural network's prediction of protein binding sites, helping biologists understand regulatory mechanisms by comparing to neutral DNA baselines.

Debugging a deep learning image classifier that misclassifies medical scans by attributing the decision to specific image regions, revealing if the model focuses on irrelevant artifacts rather than pathological features.

Providing transparent explanations for automated loan approval decisions by showing which financial features (relative to typical applicant profiles) most influenced the neural network's recommendation.

limitations.description: Requires careful selection of reference baseline, as different choices can lead to substantially different attribution scores.
Implementation complexity varies significantly across different neural network architectures and layer types.
May produce unintuitive results when the chosen reference is not representative of the decision boundary.
Limited to feedforward networks and specific layer types, not suitable for all modern architectures like transformers.

resources.title: Learning Important Features Through Propagating Activation Differences
resources.abstract: The purported "black box" nature of neural networks is a barrier to adoption in applications where interpretability is essential. Here we present DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures), a method for decomposing the output prediction of a neural network on a specific input by backpropagating the contributions of all neurons in the network to every feature of the input. DeepLIFT compares the activation of each neuron to its 'reference activation' and assigns contribution scores according to the difference. By optionally giving separate consideration to positive and negative contributions, DeepLIFT can also reveal dependencies which are missed by other approaches. Scores can be computed efficiently in a single backward pass. We apply DeepLIFT to models trained on MNIST and simulated genomic data, and show significant advantages over gradient-based methods. Video tutorial: http://goo.gl/qKb7pL, ICML slides: bit.ly/deeplifticmlslides, ICML talk: https://vimeo.com/238275076, code: http://goo.gl/RM8jvH.

resources.title: An Attribution Deep Learning Interpretation Model for Landslide Susceptibility Mapping in the Three Gorges Reservoir Area
resources.abstract: Deep learning (DL) models are increasingly used for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) due to their higher accuracy. However, due to the lack of explanations of the influence of input contributing factors by current DL models, accurately identifying the cause of each landslide remains challenging. This study proposes a novel interpretable DL model named Deep-Attention-LSF, which assigns significance scores to contributing factors at local levels for attributing landslide susceptibility. This model considers the significance scores of input factors to more accurately predict landslide occurrence. DeepLIFT is used as an attribution branching network for interpreting the relationship between input factors and each landslide event. Subsequently, a landslide classification network formed by combining convolutional neural network and long short-term memory is used to predict the landslide occurrence in the entire study area. The performance of Deep-Attention-LSF is tested using the landslide inventory map of Three Gorges reservoir area and the associated maps of 18 landslide-related factors. The accuracy, recall, precision, and F1-score of our model were 0.9645, 0.9583, 0.9676, and 0.9522, respectively. These suggest that our model outperformed the compared models, including self-attention LSM, frequency-ratio-attention LSM, bagging and random subspace naive bayes tree, gradient boosting decision tree, random forest, information value model and enhanced C5.0 decision tree model. Deep-Attention-LSF provided reasonable explanations for landslide attributions by comparison with field investigation reports for four specific landslide cases. Combining the interpretation of Deep-Attention-LSF with field investigations can provide more comprehensive information for evaluating specific landslides, providing a useful tool for landslide prevention and management.

techniques.name: Synthetic Data Evaluation
techniques.description: Synthetic data evaluation checks whether an artificial dataset made to stand in for sensitive real records is safe to share and still useful, and reports the trade-off between the two. Privacy is tested by simulating an attacker who holds the synthetic data and some facts about a person, and measuring how accurately the attacker can use the data to infer that person's sensitive values. Fidelity is tested by comparing the synthetic and real data column by column and in pairs of columns. Another check trains a classifier to tell the two apart, and a classifier that cannot beat chance suggests they are statistically alike. Utility is tested by running the analyses or training the models the data is meant for on the synthetic data and comparing the results with those from the real data.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital research office wants to share synthetic outpatient records with university partners. Before release it simulates an attacker who knows each patient's age band, sex and postcode district and tries to infer their diagnosis from the synthetic table, and it withholds the data if the attack does better than guessing from overall diagnosis rates.

A national statistics office gives researchers synthetic microdata for exploratory analysis. After the researchers settle on their models, the office runs the same models on the real data inside a secure environment and compares the estimates, to tell the researchers whether their exploratory conclusions can be trusted.

A bank's fraud team generates synthetic card transactions to share with an external vendor. It compares how often each fraud type appears and how amount, merchant type and time of day relate in the real and synthetic data, then checks that a model trained on the synthetic data still catches rare fraud in held-out real transactions.

limitations.description: Stronger privacy protection usually costs data quality, so the three scores pull against each other. There is no neutral threshold: where to set the balance depends on how sensitive the data is and what it will be used for, and the evaluation reports the trade-off without settling it.

Attack-based privacy tests only probe the attacks and attacker knowledge that were tried. A dataset that resists them may still leak to an attacker with more auxiliary information or a better method, so a good result is not proof of safety.

Fidelity and utility scores depend on which metrics, models and analyses are chosen. A synthetic dataset can match the real data on the columns and column pairs checked yet differ in ways that matter for a particular analysis, and general and analysis-specific utility scores can disagree.

Scores summarise the whole table, so rare events and small subgroups can be lost without moving the totals much. A fraud pattern or a minority group that the generator has smoothed away may show up only if the evaluation is designed to look for it.

The tests need statistical, privacy-engineering and domain expertise to set up and read. A classifier-based fidelity check can be misled by over-fitting or under-fitting the classifier, and weak settings can make poor synthetic data look good.

resources.title: General and Specific Utility Measures for Synthetic Data
resources.abstract: Data holders can produce synthetic versions of data sets when concerns about potential disclosure restrict the availability of the original records. The paper is concerned with methods to judge whether such synthetic data have a distribution that is comparable with that of the original data: what we term general utility. We consider how general utility compares with specific utility: the similarity of results of analyses from the synthetic data and the original data. We adapt a previous general measure of data utility, the propensity score mean-squared error pMSE, to the specific case of synthetic data and derive its distribution for the case when the correct synthesis model is used to create the synthetic data. Our asymptotic results are confirmed by a simulation study. We also consider two specific utility measures, confidence interval overlap and standardized difference in summary statistics, which we compare with the general utility results. We present two contrasting examples of data syntheses: one illustrating synthetic data that is evaluated as being useful by both general and specific measures and the second where neither is the case. For the second case we show how the general utility measures can identify the deficiencies of the synthetic data and suggest how this can inform possible improvements to the synthesis method.

resources.title: A Multifaceted benchmarking of synthetic electronic health record generation models
resources.abstract: Synthetic health data have the potential to mitigate privacy concerns in supporting biomedical research and healthcare applications. Modern approaches for data generation continue to evolve and demonstrate remarkable potential. Yet there is a lack of a systematic assessment framework to benchmark methods as they emerge and determine which methods are most appropriate for which use cases. In this work, we introduce a systematic benchmarking framework to appraise key characteristics with respect to utility and privacy metrics. We apply the framework to evaluate synthetic data generation methods for electronic health records data from two large academic medical centers with respect to several use cases. The results illustrate that there is a utility-privacy tradeoff for sharing synthetic health data and further indicate that no method is unequivocally the best on all criteria in each use case, which makes it evident why synthetic data generation methods need to be assessed in context.

resources.title: Generating and Evaluating Synthetic UK Primary Care Data: Preserving Data Utility & Patient Privacy
resources.abstract: There is increasing interest in the potential of synthetic data to validate and benchmark machine learning algorithms as well as reveal any biases in real-world data used for algorithm development. This paper discusses the key requirements of synthetic data for such purposes and proposes an approach to generating and evaluating synthetic data that meets these requirements. We propose a framework to generate and evaluate synthetic data with the aim of simultaneously preserving the complexities of ground truth data in the synthetic data whilst also ensuring privacy. We include as a case study, a proof-of-concept synthetic dataset modelled on UK primary care data to demonstrate the application of this framework.

techniques.name: Data Validation Checks
techniques.description: Data validation checks apply a written set of rules about what valid data look like to every new batch of data before a model is trained on it or uses it to make predictions, and flag or hold back any batch that breaks them. In Great Expectations (GX Core), a widely used open-source library for this, each rule is an expectation, a declarative assertion such as that a column exists and has a given type, has no missing values or takes values only from an allowed set or within a range (rules on single values can allow a stated share of rows to fail), or keeps a summary statistic (its mean, a quantile, or the divergence of its histogram from one built on reference data) within bounds the team sets. Expectations are grouped into a suite that a checkpoint runs on each batch as it arrives; the result records for every rule whether it passed and how many values broke it, with examples, configured actions can alert the team or update a human-readable report, and the pipeline can be set to stop training or scoring on a batch that failed. Running the same suite on training batches and on the data a deployed model receives catches differences between the two, such as a feature that is always missing in production, before they degrade predictions; unlike out-of-distribution detectors, the checks need no model and judge whole batches against explicit rules rather than scoring single inputs, and unlike runtime monitoring of a deployed model they act before the model sees the data. Unlike a kernel two-sample test, its distribution rules are fixed bounds set by the team, not a statistical test of whether two samples differ.

example_use_cases.description: An air navigation service provider feeds surveillance track reports into a model that predicts aircraft arrival times. Its data engineers run an expectation suite on every incoming batch, covering required fields, units, plausible ranges for altitude and ground speed, and the share of reports with missing positions, so that a sensor change that silently switched altitude from feet to metres would stop the batch before it reached the model rather than surface weeks later as worse predictions.

A weather service that retrains a statistical correction model each month on station observations validates every monthly extract first: station identifiers must come from the station list, temperatures must lie within each station's climatological limits, no variable may have more than 2 per cent missing values, and each variable's mean and quantiles must stay within bounds set from earlier years. A failed check stops the retraining and opens a ticket listing the failing stations.

A hospital running a deterioration-risk model on laboratory results checks each hourly batch from the laboratory system against expectations for test codes, units and value ranges, so that if a laboratory changes the unit of a test without notice the batch is flagged and risk scores for the affected patients are withheld until the mapping is corrected.

A bank's credit-scoring team runs the expectation suite written for its training data on a daily sample of the applications its deployed model scores and compares the results, so that a field the online form has stopped collecting, which the scoring service quietly fills with a default value, shows up as a difference between training and production data rather than as an unexplained drop in approval rates.

limitations.description: Checks catch only what someone thought to write down. A batch can satisfy every rule and still be wrong in a way no rule covers, such as a changed relationship between two columns or a change in how labels were assigned. GX Core does not infer rules from the data, since its automatic profilers were removed in version 1.0, so each rule has to be specified, and for pipelines with thousands of features that effort can put teams off setting up validation at all.

Bounds for distribution rules are hard to set. Statistical tests on large batches fire on differences too small to matter: in Google's data validation paper, a chi-square test between 100 million points and a copy with 0.01 per cent of them redrawn from a wider distribution raised an alert in 7 of 10 trials, while thresholds on divergence measures such as KL divergence are hard for teams to interpret. Bounds are therefore tuned by trial, risking too many alerts or missed shifts.

The rules describe the input data, not the model's performance. A batch that passes can still produce wrong predictions if the relationship between inputs and outcomes has changed (concept drift), and a batch that fails shows that the data changed, not that predictions got worse, so the checks need pairing with monitoring of performance once outcomes arrive.

Alerts help only if someone acts on them, and rules need upkeep as data legitimately change. In Google's deployment across more than 700 pipelines, new columns, unexpected values and missing columns were the commonest anomalies, most pipelines revised their schema, and between 28 and 100 per cent of fired anomalies of each kind were fixed, which the authors attribute partly to operators missing or ignoring alerts.

The checks work on tables: GX Core connects to data frames, SQL databases and data files, so for images, audio, free text or gridded weather fields the team must first compute a table of properties, such as sizes, value ranges or missing tiles, and write rules about those. This catches broken or truncated inputs but not changes in what the content shows.

techniques.name: Kernel Two-Sample Test (Maximum Mean Discrepancy)
techniques.description: A kernel two-sample test checks whether two sets of data could have come from the same distribution; in assurance it is used to check whether the inputs a deployed model now receives still resemble the data on which it was validated, and to detect when they stop doing so. Its statistic, the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), is built from a kernel, a function that scores how similar two data points are (commonly a Gaussian function of the distance between them), and in its usual squared form it is the average similarity among points in the reference sample, plus the average similarity among points in the new sample, minus twice the average similarity between points from different samples. With a characteristic kernel such as the Gaussian, the population value is zero only when the two distributions are identical, so the test can respond to any kind of difference, including a change in how features vary together that tests applied to one feature at a time cannot see, and kernels exist for strings and graphs as well as numerical vectors. To obtain a p-value, the two samples are pooled and repeatedly divided at random into groups of the original sizes, the statistic is recomputed for each division, and the p-value is the share of divisions giving a value at least as large as the one observed; high-dimensional inputs such as images are usually first reduced to a short vector, for example the code of an autoencoder or the model's predicted class probabilities. The output, for each window of new data, is the MMD value and its p-value at a stated significance level, which shows whether that window differs detectably from the reference, but not whether the difference affects the model's accuracy.

example_use_cases.description: A card issuer's model-risk team tests a random sample of each night's transactions, at most one per customer, against a fixed sample from the fraud model's validation period, after standardising the input features. It set the significance level so that, with nothing changed, it expects about one false alarm a quarter, and a significant result triggers a check of the model's accuracy on newly labelled cases before its alert thresholds are relied on the next day.

Before switching on a chest X-ray triage model at a second hospital that uses a different make of scanner, the deploying team compares 500 recent images from the new site with 500 from the validation set. Each image is first reduced to a short vector by an autoencoder trained on validation images. A significant difference sends the model for local validation on labelled cases from the new site instead of relying on its original results.

A customer-service team whose question-answering assistant was evaluated on a fixed test set compares the sentence embeddings of each week's user questions with those of the test set. When a week is flagged, it computes the MMD witness function, which scores each question by how much more it resembles the new week's questions than the test set, reads the top-scoring questions, finds queries about a new product, and adds such questions to the test set.

limitations.description: A significant result shows that inputs differ from the reference, not that the model has got worse: Rabanser et al. note that distributions shift constantly and often harmlessly, and with large windows the test can flag differences too small to matter. A drift alarm becomes evidence about performance only when followed by an accuracy check on labelled cases, and an absence of alarms reassures only if the test was shown beforehand to detect the shifts that harm the model.

On raw high-dimensional inputs the test has little power: in Rabanser et al.'s comparison on image data the multivariate test performed poorly without first reducing the dimension. The reduction then decides what can be seen, since a change that leaves the autoencoder code or predicted probabilities unchanged goes undetected. The kernel's width matters too: it is usually set to the median distance between points, which Gretton et al. call a heuristic, the best width being an open question.

The statistic compares every pair of points, so its cost grows with the square of the combined sample size, and the permutation test repeats it many times; Rabanser et al. ran kernel tests only up to 1,000 new samples for this reason. Gretton et al.'s linear-time version is far cheaper but needs much more data for the same power, so high-volume monitoring has to trade window size, detection delay and computing cost against each other.

The permutation p-value assumes that observations within each sample are independent. Consecutive sensor readings, transactions from one customer or successive time steps are correlated, and shuffling them breaks that dependence, so the test signals a difference far more often than its stated level: in Chwialkowski et al.'s experiments on autocorrelated signals the permutation test almost always rejected when nothing had changed. Such data need thinning or a wild bootstrap.

Run on every new window at the conventional 5 per cent level, the test flags about one window in twenty even when nothing has changed, which for daily windows means around 18 false alarms a year. Continuous monitoring needs a stricter level, a correction for repeated testing, or an online version of the test whose threshold is set for an expected run time between false alarms.

resources.title: A Kernel Two-Sample Test
resources.abstract: We propose a framework for analyzing and comparing distributions, which we use to construct statistical tests to determine if two samples are drawn from different distributions.  Our test statistic is the largest difference in expectations over functions in the unit ball of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), and is called the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD).  We present two distribution-free tests based on large deviation bounds for the MMD, and a third test based on the asymptotic distribution of this statistic.  The MMD can be computed in quadratic time, although efficient linear time approximations are available.  Our statistic is an instance of an integral probability metric, and various classical metrics on distributions are obtained when alternative function classes are used in place of an RKHS.  We apply our two-sample tests  to a variety of problems, including attribute matching for databases using the Hungarian marriage method, where they perform strongly.  Excellent performance is also obtained when comparing distributions over graphs, for which these are the first such tests.

Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift
resources.abstract: We might hope that when faced with unexpected inputs, well-designed software systems would fire off warnings. Machine learning (ML) systems, however, which depend strongly on properties of their inputs (e.g. the i.i.d. assumption), tend to fail silently. This paper explores the problem of building ML systems that fail loudly, investigating methods for detecting dataset shift, identifying exemplars that most typify the shift, and quantifying shift malignancy. We focus on several datasets and various perturbations to both covariates and label distributions with varying magnitudes and fractions of data affected. Interestingly, we show that across the dataset shifts that we explore, a two-sample-testing-based approach, using pre-trained classifiers for dimensionality reduction, performs best. Moreover, we demonstrate that domain-discriminating approaches tend to be helpful for characterizing shifts qualitatively and determining if they are harmful.

sample_claims.text: Applied to autoencoder representations of 500 images from each source, the kernel two-sample test found no significant difference at the 1 per cent level between the new hospital's chest X-rays and the validation images, and the same test detected the simulated scanner changes that had reduced the model's accuracy in validation.

Every alarm raised by the nightly kernel two-sample test on the fraud model's inputs in the past six months was followed within two working days by an accuracy check on newly labelled cases, and each check either met the accuracy requirement or led to retraining.

In each weekly window since deployment, the loan-application model's production inputs showed no difference from its validation sample detectable by the agreed kernel two-sample test, at a significance level corrected for weekly repetition, and the same test detected the input shifts that had reduced the model's accuracy in pre-deployment trials.
Replayed on reference data alone, the drift monitor's kernel two-sample test raised false alarms at no more than the configured rate of one per quarter.

techniques.name: TimeSHAP
techniques.description: TimeSHAP explains one prediction of a model that reads a sequence of events, such as a recurrent neural network that scores a bank transaction using the account's history, by giving each past event, each input feature and selected event-feature cells a Shapley value: a share of the score, taken from cooperative game theory, such that all the shares add up to the difference between the model's score and its score with every event and feature removed. It adapts KernelSHAP, the sampling estimator in SHAP, which explains a single input vector and so, applied to the latest event of a recurrent model, gives earlier events no credit; TimeSHAP instead switches off whole rows or columns of the event-by-feature input matrix, replacing them with a background value (the training-data average in the original paper), queries the model on many such perturbed sequences, and fits a weighted linear model whose coefficients are the attributions. Because the number of event combinations doubles with every event, a pruning step first walks back from the most recent event and merges all older events into a single player once their combined attribution falls below a chosen tolerance, and cell-level values are computed only where the most important events and features intersect, with the other cells grouped. The model is treated as a black box that takes a batch of sequences and returns one score per sequence, and the output is event, feature and cell attributions for each explained sequence, plus plots that aggregate them across many sequences into a global view.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's fraud operations team runs TimeSHAP on each alert from its recurrent account-takeover model, so the analyst reviewing an alert sees which earlier events (for example a password change, then a login from a new device) and which features carried the score, not only the payment being held. The analyst uses this to decide whether to release the payment or contact the customer, and the model team samples the explanations to check that the drivers match known fraud patterns.

A hospital data-science team validating a recurrent model that predicts next-day escalation of treatment for patients in intensive care computes event- and feature-level TimeSHAP values for test-set patients and reviews them with clinicians. Drivers the clinicians judge implausible, such as an indicator that a measurement is missing outweighing the measurements themselves, are investigated before the model is used in a prospective study.

An airport's forecasting team using a recurrent model to warn of fog in the next six hours from the past 48 hours of station observations uses the pruning statistics and global event plots to find how far back the model actually draws on, and the feature attributions to check that humidity, temperature and wind lead each warning. The findings set the input window for the next retraining and go into the model's validation report.

limitations.description: Every attribution is measured against the background chosen to stand for a removed event or feature, the training-data average in the original paper. A sequence containing averaged events may be unlike anything the model has seen, and another background gives other attributions; the original authors note that a feature scoring zero for every sequence may reflect the background rather than the model. Report the background with the results.

Exact values need every combination of events, which doubles with each event. On the original fraud data (median sequence about 138 events), exact values were possible for only 10% of sequences with 32,000 sampled combinations, and repeated runs disagreed (relative standard deviation 1.71 without pruning, 0.98 at the chosen tolerance). With tens of thousands of model calls per explanation, explaining every scored event in real time is impractical; the alerts people review are the usual scope.

Pruning trades detail on older events for speed and stability. All events before the cut-off share one attribution. The cut-off test compares the older block's net, signed attribution with a user-set tolerance, so by construction an early event that pushed the score up can pass unseen if others pushed it down; the original paper does not measure how often this happens. Results change with the tolerance, so fix it in advance and report it.

It explains one score per sequence: the reference implementation expects the model to return a single value for each sequence. A model with many outputs, such as a forecast for several lead times or locations, needs a separate run or a chosen summary for each. The attributions show what the model relies on, not causes in the world: in the original study a high attribution to customer age led to a bias audit, which was needed to establish the disparity.

Each event and feature receives one number, so an effect that arises only from a combination, such as a settings change followed by a login from a new device, is shared out among its parts: an analyst sees each part with some credit but cannot tell that they matter only together. Cell-level values are computed only where the top-ranked events and features intersect. A clinical study using the method found escalation effects hard to see and suggested interactions as the cause.

techniques.name: Actionable Recourse Audit
techniques.description: An actionable recourse audit checks whether the people a linear classifier refuses, for example for a loan, a job interview or a public service, could change that decision through actions open to them, and how much they would have to change. The auditor first writes an action set saying which features can change and how: immutable features such as age stay fixed, features such as education level can only rise, and each changeable feature gets bounds and a grid of realistic values. Then, for each refused person in a sample drawn from the population the model will serve, an integer programming solver (optimisation software that searches discrete choices exactly) looks through the permitted actions for the cheapest change that flips the decision, measuring cost as the largest shift, in population percentiles, that the change makes to any one feature, and either returns that action or proves that none exists, which a search that simply fails to find a counterfactual cannot do. The audit reports the share of refused people who have recourse and the distribution of its cost, which can be compared across candidate models or broken down by group, and the same solver can list a refused person's cheapest alternative changes (a 'flipset') for a decision notice. Unlike the Contrastive Explanation Method, which explains one prediction through features that must be present or absent, or Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE), which searches any model for several alternative inputs that would change one decision, the audit works only on linear models but certifies whether any permitted action exists and summarises the answer across a population.

example_use_cases.description: Before launching a linear model that ranks applications to a housing support scheme, a local authority's analytics team audits recourse on last year's applicants, with age and household size fixed. Its report to the scheme's oversight board gives the share of refused applicants who could qualify through changes the scheme expects, such as completing a tenancy course, and how large those changes are, so the board can decide whether to approve the model.

A credit card issuer generates a flipset for each applicant its linear scorecard declines and puts the two cheapest items in the decline letter, for example reducing current debt to a stated amount, together with the other scored features the applicant should keep unchanged, so that following the stated actions would change the decision under the current model.

A lender's model risk committee is shown recourse audits for candidate credit models of almost equal accuracy. It rejects the most accurate, under which some refused applicants had no feasible action because of an 'ever defaulted' feature, adopts a variant that uses recent defaults only, and has the audit re-run each quarter on new applicants, watching younger applicants, who were scarce in the training data.

An employer's analytics team audits its linear screening model for interview invitations and compares the cost of recourse for refused women and men with similar predicted scores. Sex is not a model input, but the cost can still differ by sex. Refused candidates' true suitability is never observed, so the team cannot also match on outcome as the originating study did, and reports any gap with that caveat to its fairness review panel, which decides whether the features need revising.

limitations.description: The proof that no action exists depends on the model being linear, such as logistic regression, a linear support vector machine or a rule set that can be written in linear form. For tree ensembles or neural networks, a local linear approximation can still suggest actions, which then have to be checked on the real model, but a failure to find one proves nothing, so the share of refused people without recourse is no longer a certified figure.

Every conclusion rests on the action set and cost the auditor chooses. Bounds that are too tight make people appear to lack recourse; loose bounds let a model 'provide' recourse only through drastic changes, which shows only as high cost; and the default cost treats a one-percentile change as equally hard in every feature unless someone who knows the domain sets how much harder some changes are.

The search treats features as changing independently unless the auditor adds constraints. Real actions have knock-on effects: raising income can also raise savings, so a listed action may cost more than needed, or may not change the decision once its effects on other features are counted, as Karimi, Schölkopf and Valera showed for recourse methods that ignore causal relations between features.

Recourse is defined for a fixed model. After retraining, an action given in an earlier notice may no longer change the decision, so the audit has to be re-run after each update. An action that changes the prediction need not change the real outcome either: showing a refused applicant how to be approved can lead them into credit they cannot repay.

A flipset lists only the features to change, so a person who also changes an undisclosed feature may still be refused unless the notice says what must stay the same. The originating paper builds flipsets from public credit datasets and does not test whether refused people understand them or can act on them. Owners may also resist publishing flipsets, because many of them together can let others reconstruct the model.
